item.title: Elon Musk is preparing for a Democratic Congress and warns he'll fight back
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Elon Musk has adopted a war posture in response to looming threats of congressional investigations: If Democrats win control of Congress in next month’s midterm elections, Musk has signaled he is bracing for a fight. “Live by the sword, die by the sword,” he said Wednesday in a post on X, responding to a Politico report that cited Democratic lawmakers seeking to investigate him. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets,” said Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX. Musk’s battle-ready stance comes as a host of Democrats have said they are eager to wield the power of their office to investigate the world’s richest person should they win either chamber in the midterms. As Republicans’ election prospects have soured, lawmakers are building momentum for probes looking into the tech mogul, his companies or the work of the U.S. DOGE Service, which Musk oversaw and which was instrumental in dismantling the U.S. Agency for International Development. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (Connecticut), the ranking Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said in an interview Thursday that he would investigate Musk and DOGE if Democrats win. Blumenthal led inquiries relating to the cost-cutting group but was in the minority and did not have subpoena power, which could be used to compel the attendance of witnesses, as well as the production of documents and records. “The American people have a right to know the cost, the consequences and the chaos resulting from DOGE and … what he may be concealing,” Blumenthal said. “There is a web of potential corruption here that needs to be explored.” He dismissed Musk’s threats of retaliation, expressing surprise at his strong reaction. “He should have nothing to hide,” said Blumenthal, adding that he would expect a Democratic chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee to support efforts to investigate Musk. Musk did not respond to requests for comment. Diverging from many of his corporate peers, Musk has consistently countered threats with force. He has contested lawsuits, picked fights with powerful government officials and at times taken drastic action over business disputes, including changing his state of residence - and the locations of his businesses - from California to Texas. But Musk has also acknowledged his own vulnerability in an unfavorable political environment, joking in 2024 about the prospect of going to prison if President Donald Trump was not elected to a second term. Musk has also poured his resources into midterm races, eclipsing his donations toward Trump’s election in 2024. He is the largest individual donor in the 2026 midterm elections, putting more than $350 million toward efforts to elect Republicans. Musk and others who carried out DOGE’s agenda face a potential slew of subpoenas, investigations and hearings after the midterms, in which Democrats are heavily favored. Several other Democratic members of Congress have also raised the prospect of exploring Musk’s business or political ventures in recent days. Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Virginia), a member of the House Oversight Committee, tagged Musk in a post on X. “I’d just like you to explain to Congress and the American people why DOGE failed so miserably and why you then lied about the savings,” he wrote. “Will you commit to testifying under oath to explain?” Disputed legacy As an influential adviser to President Donald Trump last year, Musk oversaw the sweeping and at times chaotic U.S. DOGE Service campaign to cut costs at government agencies. Staffed largely with young tech workers new to government service who were chosen by Musk and his circle, DOGE eliminated the jobs of hundreds of thousands of federal workers and accessed sensitive data on hundreds of millions of Americans. Musk said that he aimed to cut $2 trillion in federal spending with DOGE, which ultimately claimed $215 billion in estimated savings. A Government Accountability Office audit found that the group consistently overstated its savings. DOGE took credit for lease cancellations set into motion before it existed, for example, and claimed savings from contracts that continued to exist. Musk has at times issued threats of retribution on X, the platform he bought in 2022 when it was named Twitter and later folded into his rocket company SpaceX. “There is a large graveyard filled with my enemies,” he wrote in a 2023 post. “I do not wish to add to it, but will if given no choice. Those who pick fights with me do so at their own peril, but maybe this is their lucky day.” The entrepreneur mused about his fate if Democrats took power in a 2024 interview with Tucker Carlson. “If he loses, I’m f---ed,” Musk said, going on to joke: “How long do you think my prison sentence is going to be?” “There may be some vengeance on me” if Trump doesn’t retake the White House, Musk said in the interview, which took place before the election. Should Democrats regain control of Congress this time, they will face pressure from some voters and activist groups to move on Musk. Activist group Investigate DOGE has channeled the spirit of the Tesla Takedown movement, which staged anti-Musk demonstrations outside Tesla showrooms, calling for Musk and DOGE alumni to face congressional scrutiny. Activists are asking, “‘How do we make sure Elon gets held accountable if Democrats take congress again?’” said Evan Sutton, a spokesman for the group. “Congress needs to get in there. They need to get their hands dirty. The American people need to know what happened.” Some former DOGE staffers are already taking precautions in the event of a Democratic-controlled Congress, seeking to insulate themselves from the potential outcomes of ethics probes by attempting to button up their post-DOGE business dealings. Though the midterms are still more than a week away, Musk continues to signal he’s readying a counteroffensive. Responding to a video of the tech journalist Kara Swisher noting that if Democrats take power, he “knows what’s coming,” Musk had a simple reply: “Message received.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/23/musk-says-he-will-fight-back-if-congressional-democrats-investigate-doge/

item.title: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions remain despite Trump's claims they're lifted
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Ukraine is still recording issues with the Starlink internet network, sources within the defence ministry say, after Donald Trump said limits had been reversed by Elon Musk who owns the satellite system. The sources told the BBC that instances of drones experiencing connection loss at speeds of 161km/h (100mph) were being recorded, hampering military operations. The US president had denied instructing the tech billionaire to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying on Thursday that Musk had "put it back". Asked on Friday, Trump said: "If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out." Trump added: "I have not spoken to him. I might have to, but I have not. I've heard it was fixed, but if it's not, I'll speak to him." Musk previously said he was not behind the slowdown, which affected Ukraine's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations. Trump told reporters he did not think the tech billionaire had too much power. The Ukrainian defence ministry sources said the military was constantly monitoring the performance of both the Starlink and Starshield networks. They added that there was "currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted". Last week, Kyiv said uplink speeds to the low Earth orbit satellites had been restricted, affecting the speed at which drones could travel. Any drone travelling faster than 100mph lost its connection, officials said. Shortly after, Musk said that Starshield , which Ukraine uses for some of its operation, was controlled by the US military and suggested that the Pentagon could be behind the issues. The White House has since repeatedly denied deliberately placing limits on the network in Ukraine. In a call with Trump on Friday evening, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham "underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", Downing Street said in a statement. Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones. Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. One Ukrainian soldier said there was "simply no alternative" to Starshield, adding that earlier in the week, connectivity had been cutting out when his unit had been travelling in a car at 80km/h (50 mph). "I'll tell you this much: God forbid they shut it off completely - it would be an absolute catastrophe," he told the BBC. "We need a backup option for securing communications and internet." Another soldier said they had reverted to the "proven algorithms" they used before they had Starlink when it initially started playing up, but stressed that Ukrainian forces did need the network, citing its speed. "Even one or two seconds is critical when we can transfer data and orders faster," she said. "You can really feel that advantage on the battlefield." Ukrainian reports of a slowdown to the service came during a tense diplomatic row between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies. [BBC] Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher. While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war . Zelensky said the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump later denied. The row prompted a war of words between the two world leaders, with Trump suggesting it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and Zelensky implying Trump was not a real leader. Earlier on Thursday - before Trump's comments - Zelensky had said the speed of the system had still not been restored fully. "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so." The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had told Musk that he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped, and that the system was working closer to normal following that conversation. item.title: Wells Fargo says customers may be liable for unwanted purchases by their AI agents
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Citi Bank, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase have taken steps to limit third-party AI agents from accessing their platforms and services, and others are following suit. The banks’ decisions, first reported by Axios , come amid mounting concern over AI agents taking unwanted actions on behalf of users. Two-thirds of chief information security officers surveyed in financial services and software ranked agentic AI among their top three cybersecurity risks, and more than one-third named it as their top concern, according to a 2026 study by Palo Alto Networks . “We do not permit third-party AI agents or assistants to log into a customer's account or transact directly within our digital banking platforms,” a Citi spokesperson wrote to USA TODAY. Citi customers can authorize agents to “limited, read-only access to their account information with certain Citi-approved open banking providers,” the statement continued. Citi has not seen reports of agents accessing client accounts. “There’s a window of vulnerability where the systems, the banks, the users are all vulnerable to the speed with which AI is being weaponized,” said Andre Durand, founder and CEO of Ping Identity, which sells identity security infrastructure to financial institutions. He cited concern over AI being used to perpetrate fraud and scams at higher levels as well as fear that agents could be compromised or decide to take malicious action on their own. In an October report by Ping , 71% of consumers surveyed reported concern that an AI agent acting on their behalf could misrepresent their personality or values. However, less than a quarter said they refuse to trust AI with any financial transaction, at 22%. Durand said that “the challenge that we're having right now is how can we detect that it is an agent and not a human asking. And if we can detect that it’s an agent not a human, how do we know that the agent is acting on the authority of the human?” Agent restrictions Bank of America, Capital One and four other global banks created a coalition in September to warn that agentic technology is moving faster than industry standards and protections are keeping up. The coalition highlighted the risk that AI shopping agents pose in particular. “When you give the agent your credentials, it is you authorizing the payment. So we’re just trying to work with these companies and with the industry to say, put a human being in the loop,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told Bloomberg on Oct. 15. “So before you pay, you authorize it, so that we know that you know you’re paying for something.” According to Moynihan, Bank of America is restricting AI agents’ access to consumer deposits and is working with companies to develop protocols on agents. JPMorgan Chase CEO confirmed to Bloomberg last week that JPMorgan Chase is also blocking outside agents from accessing customer-account information. Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase did not immediately respond to a request for comment from USA TODAY. Wells Fargo has also “taken steps to block unauthorized agents from accessing customer accounts,” a bank spokesperson told USA TODAY. According to Wells Fargo’s updated online access agreement , authorized representative or delegate transactions – including transactions of agents – are considered authorized, unless the user explicitly tells the bank they are not authorized and the bank “have had reasonable opportunity to act on your notification.” The agreement is set to take effect on Nov. 24. It includes a section on third-party AI agents in which users agree that they are "solely responsible” for supervising agents, that the bank may act on the instructions of agents and that all transactions taken by authorized representatives such as agents – “including those you did not want or intend” – are considered authorized. “If you permit an AI Agent or other third party access to the Service, you acknowledge that doing so may adversely impact the commercially reasonable security procedures that you've otherwise agreed to, and you accept the risk of such access,” according to the agreement. Durand said he wasn’t aware of specific instances of agents hacking into banks, but added, “I don’t think a lot of stuff is being reported” in regards to agents or AI activity at banks. Alternative options In addition to blocking unauthorized agents from logging in on behalf of clients, Charles Schwab created its own AI assistant , called Charley, which cannot execute trades but can answer questions and complete routine tasks. Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said in an interview with Bloomberg on Oct. 16 that the bank is blocking between “tens and twenties” of attempts by major AI agents to access and manipulate client funds. As AI agent usage grows — Meta reported that Muse grew to 10 million users on Oct. 21 — Durand emphasized the need for better authentication systems. One-time passwords sent to emails are no longer secure enough, he said, because agents often have access to email. “Passkeys and biometrics ensure that the human is the one authenticating, and/or that the human is the one authorizing,” Durand said. Greta Reich covers the artificial intelligence industry for USA TODAY through a fellowship from the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism. Funders do not provide editorial input. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: ‘Window of vulnerability’: Banks move to restrict AI agent access This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2026/10/23/banks-move-to-limit-ai-agent-access/92385119007/

item.title: Democrats are favored to flip the House, but Republicans still have a path to victory
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It's crunch time. With less than two weeks to go until the 2026 midterm elections, Democratic and Republican candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives nationwide are making one last push to persuade voters in their districts — and help their party win or retain control of the chamber on Nov. 3. The stakes are high. President Trump has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block parts of the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again) . Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. But the past doesn't necessarily predict the future, and Republicans have certain advantages today that they didn't have before. Here's what needs to happen for each party to come out on top. Yahoo The races to watch The first thing to know about any House election is that while all 435 congressional districts are technically up for grabs, roughly 80% of those contests (representing about 350 seats) are not considered competitive. House incumbents have always had huge advantages: money and name recognition, mostly. But their head start has only widened in recent years as partisan polarization and redistricting have helped make the vast majority of congressional districts "safe" for one party . These days, incumbents tend to focus more on fending off primary challengers. The general election can be a breeze in comparison. As a result, this year's true battleground is relatively small. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report's " race ratings ," just 17 contests are genuine "tossups" at this point. Another 16 "lean Democratic," and 17 "lean Republican." There's also a third competitive category that includes 18 seats where Democrats are the "likely" winners, and 13 seats where the same could be said about Republicans. That's 81 competitive districts — again, out of 435. It's clear from looking at this year's ratings which party is playing more defense and which is playing more offense — and where. Only 30 Democratic seats are considered competitive, and more than half of them (17) are "likely" to remain Democratic, according to Cook. Just five Democratic seats are tossups. Just two are leaning Republican. In contrast, a full 51 Republican seats are considered competitive — and about half of them are tossups (12) or leaning Democratic (12). Geographically, this year's tossups are concentrated in certain kinds of places: Rust Belt districts in states that have swung from party to party in the past (such as Michigan, Pennsylvania and Ohio); Mid-Atlantic suburbs (in states such as New York, Virginia and North Carolina) where Trump has scrambled some of the usual coalitions; and Sun Belt districts (think Florida, Texas, California and Nevada) where Latinos factor heavily. Trump carried many of these areas in 2024 . On Friday, Cook shifted another 19 of its race ratings toward Democrats — part of a pattern that has seen the outlet move a total of 63 race ratings toward Democrats over the last month. "Republicans' path to keeping control of the House has all but evaporated," Cook's House analyst wrote . "Following this latest round of ratings changes, Democrats now are favored outright in the 218 seats they need to win control of the House. In other words, 220 seats are rated either Solid, Likely or Lean Democrat. Republicans, meanwhile, are favored in 198 seats, rated Solid, Likely, or Lean Republican." Overall, the map gives Democrats more pickup options — which means more paths to a House majority. The path to a Democratic House Senate and governor contests can be quirky — more state-specific and personality-driven. But national dynamics tend to play a larger role in shaping the composition of the incoming House. So it's not just a matter of who has more targets on the board. It's that the board itself tends to tilt to one side or the other, taking most of those targets with it. A recent example was the 2010 midterm election, when impatience with America's slow recovery from the 2008 financial collapse and frustration with President Barack Obama's response helped Republicans gain 64 House seats. Beyond the history of midterm backlash against the president's party, Democrats have two big advantages right now. One is that the current Republican majority is so minuscule — just 219 votes to 214, including an independent who caucuses with Republicans — that Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to win back the House. The other is that the board seems to be tilting in Democrats' favor — assuming the polls are right. Surveys suggest there's one underlying factor pulling the national electorate to the left: dissatisfaction with Trump. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , an average of 60% of Americans currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 37% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -23% — near his all-time low. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 71% disapprove and 25% approve . That's a 46-point gap. President Trump arrives to speak at a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena on Oct. 10, 2026, in Clarksville, Tenn. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Democrats aren't particularly popular. But for the party in power, it may be hard to overcome this level of dissatisfaction with the status quo. That's why, when pollsters ask their so-called generic ballot question — If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? — Americans are currently giving Democrats a substantial lead of more than 9 percentage points , on average. Making matters worse for Republicans, that lead has grown over the last month as swing voters who favored Trump in 2024 — including some Latinos and independents — say they're planning to vote Democratic. To put a 9-point lead in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7.6 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. On Election Day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. If the polls are right, Democrats might win control of the House again. The path to a Republican House But are the polls right? Recently, Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side — including Democratic leads in rural red states such as Iowa , Kansas and Nebraska — to argue that pollsters might be misjudging public sentiment. They're not wrong to say the polls have missed in the past. Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another . The Trump era has been a little different. In each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver . The theory is that a phenomenon called nonresponse bias — in which Democratic voters are more eager or available to respond to pollsters than Republican voters — might have made Democratic support look stronger than it actually was. Pollsters try to adjust for this by weighting their results — that is, using statistical methods to give less weight to respondents who are overrepresented demographically and more weight to respondents who are underrepresented demographically. But it's difficult to predict in advance who will show up on Election Day. This time around, there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states . Could that mean Republican candidates in those places will outperform their polling? Possibly. But experts say it may also mean that rural Republicans are less supportive of the GOP than they were in 2024 — potentially voting Democratic or staying home on Nov. 3. A voter walks toward his polling place. REUTERS / REUTERS After all, there's been virtually no polling bias toward Democrats in Trump era elections when Trump himself wasn't on the ballot. In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver . Either way, pollsters aren't seeing signs of this rural effect in most states — and even if they were, it might make only a minor dent in Democrats' 9-point national lead . Redistricting is the other Republican advantage. House redistricting efforts typically take place every 10 years, after each new census reveals changes in population distribution. But last summer, Trump successfully pushed GOP legislators in Texas to pass new congressional district boundaries five years earlier than normal to help Republicans win five additional House seats in 2026. This kicked off a tit-for-tat cycle that saw nine states adopt new congressional maps for the midterms — some to benefit Democrats, others Republicans. Now that the dust has settled, Cook projects that Republicans could win nine seats because of redistricting (in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas), while Democrats could win five (in California and Utah). If that plays out, it would net the GOP four seats overall. It's not what Republicans initially hoped to gain from gerrymandering. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," GOP House Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota told Axios recently . But it's also not nothing. The hope for the GOP is that some combination of polling error and redistricting boost — along with a late influx of hundreds of millions of dollars to help defend districts Trump won in 2024 — will be just enough to preserve their slim House majority. item.title: 2 former FBI officials charged with lying to Congress about Hunter Biden laptop probe
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jeanine Pirro, U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia. (Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty ) WASHINGTON — Two former FBI officials who have come under withering criticism from allies of President Donald Trump have been charged with allegedly lying to Congress over the investigation into former President Joe Biden’s son Hunter Biden . A court docket shows that Nikki Floris, the former deputy assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence Division, and Bradley Benavides, another FBI official, were facing one count of the rarely-charged criminal offense which can be difficult to prosecute. Hunter Biden was investigated, charged and eventually convicted of gun and tax crimes, before his father pardoned him shortly leaving office. U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in a social media post that Floris and Benavides had surrendered Friday morning. She alleged that the duo lied about their roles in the Foreign Influence Task Force and “about their roles in the FBI’s Hunter Biden investigations.” Attorneys for Floris said in a statement that Floris was “a patriot” who “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years” and was charged so the administration could “push a false narrative for a shot at political points.” Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on Oct. 22, 2019. (Susan Walsh / AP) Attorneys Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle R. Freeny said in a statement that the “DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.” One of the attorneys for Benavides, Ronald S. Safer, called the charges a disgrace and said Friday that his client “worked tirelessly to protect the public from terrorists and agents of foreign governments” for 20 years and “protected our democracy against those who would destroy it.” “In return, today, the government that he loves brought baseless criminal charges against him in a transparently political complaint,” Safer said. “This is another sad day for the Department of Justice. But now we are in court, and the truth will come out: Brad Benavides is a true patriot who devoted his career to protecting this country and its people.” Trump commented on the case Friday evening while speaking to reporters in Florida. “I don’t know exactly what it is, but I heard they were arrested or charged. And I heard they were bad people,” Trump said. “You know, they’re crooked people. You know what they are? Dirty cops, like Comey.” The Trump administration is pursuing a separate case against former FBI Director James Comey, a frequent target of Trump’s, over a photo he posted on Instagram, and later deleted, of seashells arranged to spell out “8647” that prosecutors said amounted to a threat against the president. Comey has not yet entered a plea in the case but has said it did not occur to him that the numbers could be interpreted in a violent way . Asked on Friday evening if he believes the FBI was protecting the Bidens before the 2020 election, Trump said, “Yeah, I guess.” The case against the two former FBI officials was brought through a criminal complaint. Neither defendant has yet been indicted by a federal grand jury in D.C., where grand jurors have been skeptical of cases brought during Trump’s second term. Earlier this year, federal grand jurors rejected an attempt to indict six sitting Democratic members of Congress over a video Trump criticized. Flores was the FBI’s security lead for the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed was stolen. A mob of Trump supporters violently broke into the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, in a failed effort to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden as president. They beat and bloodied law enforcement, shattered windows and broke through barriers. She joined the FBI as an intelligence analyst in 2005, working on the director’s daily briefing staff and helped produce intelligence documents. She was promoted in 2017 to the department’s counterterrorism division. Benavides is a former colleague of Floris who focused on election security, foreign influence and Chinese intelligence threats. Floris has also been under criticism from Republicans over emails in which she discussed intelligence work that were obtained by Congress and declassified in July by Trump. Republicans have alleged that FBI officials buried what they describe as a credible report on China’s efforts to influence the election in an effort to protect then-FBI Director Christopher Wray. Intelligence officials and her legal team have said the pullback was a standard administrative move for a report that may have been unverified or had flawed intelligence. item.title: Kushner pushes back on report involving phone, spies, transfer
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jared Kushner is pushing back on a report involving a hacked iPhone, international spies and billion-dollar transfers from foreign governments. An upcoming book by journalist Matthew Cole claims Kushner, who is President Trump's son-in-law, had access to more than $2 billion in "slush money funds" from Middle Eastern leaders in an attempt to influence U.S. foreign policy. An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period. Kushner and his legal team released fiery statements Thursday night categorically denying all accusations against him. Kushner said , "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." His attorney called them "false and defamatory" and said they intend to pursue legal action against those responsible, but did not specify whom. The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government." An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well. According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it." At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy. The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank. According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict. The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit." Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." "We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said. "No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said. item.title: DOJ gives California counties 48 hours to help identify suspected noncitizen voters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Los Angeles (AP) — Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens , according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press. The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Donald Trump's Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare , difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. Earlier this month, the federal government targeted Los Angeles County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of roughly 20,000 people who are “likely” noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday. The Trump administration asked the 9th Circuit court of appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday. Now, according to the LA County registrar’s office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They have been given a 48 hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified. “Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli. The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including social security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more. That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county. California’s secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government’s demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens. Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted. The letters on Friday came on the heels of statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/doj-orders-california-counties-verify-012927044.html

item.title: Judge rules Jane Doe in Cornell case can remain anonymous while pursuing lawsuit
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A judge in New York on Friday decided the former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe can pursue her sexual assault claim against the university and seven fraternity members while remaining anonymous. Permission to proceed in litigation under a pseudonym is not automatic, but the judge said "the notoriety of the allegations and widespread reports of certain malicious actors' behavior" warranted anonymity. Jane Doe says she felt 'unsupported and disbelieved' by Cornell president The judge's decision came with a warning to those who have threatened Jane Doe and others connected to the case. "While the Court is cognizant that some members of the public have made it their mission to try and identify Jane Doe, and have likewise tried to use what they believe to be Jane Doe's identity to harass and threaten certain individuals allegedly tied to her, the Court issues the following words of caution: cyberstalking and engaging in or encouraging threats across state lines, whether it be of Jane Doe, any of the named defendants, or their attorneys, can be considered a federal crime and perpetrators of those acts may be subjecting themselves to prosecution," Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond wrote in her opinion. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images - PHOTO: A hand written sign is seen before a rally in support of a former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe at the Ithaca Commons, October 13, 2026 in Ithaca, New York. Former Cornell fraternity president dropped from Jane Doe lawsuit Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit alleging she had been drugged and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. All seven men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing and no criminal charges have been filed in the case. Her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, has previously told ABC News that Jane Doe and her family have been subjected to threats, doxxing and other forms of harassment. New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was appointed by Gov. Kathy Hochul, is conducting an investigation into the incident. Cornell, which said it fully supports the appointment of a special prosecutor, is also conducting an internal probe of its response to the allegations. The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country. Cornell has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies." At the same time, the university has said it is committed to taking additional steps to improve campus safety. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/US/jane-doe-cornell-lawsuit-remain-anonymous-judge-warns/story?id=137524611

item.title: U.S. intelligence warns Iranian plots to kill Americans are in 'advanced stages'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries. The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen. "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote. The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent. Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo. Axios was first to report on the memo. The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported. "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region." A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats. Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more. Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks. Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/iran-target-u-s-personnel/
